propositions.text: The applicant is a 34-year-old Ghanaian citizen who applied for a study permit in April 2025 to pursue the IEMBP at UBC.
propositions.quote: The applicant is a 34-year-old citizen of Ghana. In April 2025, she applied for a study permit in order to pursue the Internationally Educated Midwives Bridging Program (IEMBP) at the University of British Columbia.

propositions.text: Applicant was working as a Senior Staff Midwife in Ghana and planned a one-year unpaid leave to attend the program.
propositions.quote: The applicant was already working as a Senior Staff Midwife at a hospital in Ghana and planned to take a one-year unpaid leave of absence from her position.

propositions.text: Applicant explained the program would provide valuable skills to apply upon return to Ghana.
propositions.quote: She explained in her study permit application that the program would provide her with valuable skills and training that she would be able to apply when she returned to Ghana to continue working as a midwife.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is a 34-year-old Ghanaian midwife who applied for a study permit to attend the IEMBP at UBC, planning a one-year leave.

propositions.text: The IEMBP requires 12 weeks online courses and 22 weeks clinical placements in Vancouver.
propositions.quote: The IEMBP is a hybrid program where students are required to complete 12 weeks of online courses followed by at least 22 weeks of clinical placements in Vancouver.

propositions.text: Applicant completed online portion and paid nearly two-thirds of fees before applying for study permit to complete clinical training in Vancouver.
propositions.quote: The applicant had already completed the online portion of the program and paid nearly two-thirds of her total program fees before submitting her study permit application in order to complete the in-person clinical training in Vancouver between January and June, 2026.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the IEMBP is hybrid; applicant completed online part and paid most fees before applying to complete clinical training in Vancouver.

propositions.text: Visa officer refused the application on May 12, 2025, for lack of satisfaction applicant would leave Canada after authorized stay.
propositions.quote: On May 12, 2025, a visa officer with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada refused the application because the officer was not satisfied that the applicant would leave Canada at the end of her authorized stay, as required by paragraph 216(10(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker refused the applicant's study permit on May 12, 2025, doubting she would leave Canada after her stay.

propositions.text: Applicant applies for judicial review under IRPA subsection 72(1) and contends the decision is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The applicant now applies for judicial review of this decision under subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA). She contends that the decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: Court does not agree the decision is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: As I will explain, I do not agree.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant seeks judicial review claiming unreasonableness; the court disagrees with that claim.

propositions.text: The officer's decision is reviewed on a reasonableness standard requiring justification based on facts and law (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: The parties agree, as do I, that the substance of the officer’s decision is to be reviewed on a reasonableness standard. Reasonableness review aims to reinforce a “culture of justification” requiring an administrative decision maker to provide an explanation for the result that is “based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 2 and 85).

propositions.text: To set aside a decision as unreasonable, serious shortcomings must exist in justification, intelligibility, and transparency (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: To set aside the decision on the basis that it is unreasonable, the reviewing court must be satisfied that “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” (Vavilov, at para 100).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the reasonableness standard and criteria for setting aside a decision under Vavilov.

propositions.text: Judicial review principles for study permits include applicant's onus to prove legal requirements and consideration of push-pull factors (Jafarkhani).
propositions.quote: The key principles that guide judicial review of study permit decisions on a reasonableness standard are well established: see Jafarkhani v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2024 FC 1633 at para 5 and the cases cited therein. These principles include the following: The onus is on an applicant to satisfy the officer that they meet the legal requirements for obtaining a study permit, including that they will leave Canada at the end of their authorized stay.

propositions.text: Visa officers must consider push and pull factors influencing applicant's likelihood to overstay or return home.
propositions.quote: Visa officers must consider the “push” and “pull” factors that could, on the one hand, lead an applicant to overstay their visa and remain in Canada or that would, on the other hand, encourage them to return to their home country when required to.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review must consider administrative context including volume, interests, and reapplication possibility.
propositions.quote: In assessing the reasonableness of the decision, the administrative context in which it was made must be taken into account. This includes the high volume of applications to be processed, the nature of the interests involved, and the fact that often an applicant can simply reapply.

propositions.text: Use of templates by decision makers is acceptable if reasons are reasonable and justified (Ekpenyong).
propositions.quote: In and of itself, there is nothing wrong with decision makers using templates to prepare their reasons, as long as the reasons given, when read in their legal and factual context, provide a reasonable explanation for the decision (Ekpenyong v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2019 FC 1245 at paras 22-23).

propositions.text: Reasons need not be lengthy but must set out key elements and be responsive to central application aspects.
propositions.quote: Reasons do not need to be lengthy or detailed. Nevertheless, they must set out the key elements of the officer’s line of analysis and be responsive to the central aspects of the application.

propositions.text: Decision maker must justify conclusions transparently and intelligibly (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: The decision maker must “justify to the affected party, in a manner that is transparent and intelligible, the basis on which it arrived at a particular conclusion” (Vavilov, at para 96).

propositions.text: Reviewing court should not substitute its own reasons or justification for administrative decisions (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: Even if the outcome may be justifiable, “it is not ordinarily appropriate for the reviewing court to fashion its own reasons in order to buttress the administrative decision” or to “disregard the flawed basis for a decision and substitute its own justification for the outcome” (Vavilov, at para 96).

paragraphs.summary: The court outlines established principles for judicial review of study permit decisions, emphasizing reasonableness and administrative context.

propositions.text: The officer refused the application because they were not satisfied the applicant would leave Canada after authorized stay.
propositions.quote: As noted, the officer refused the study permit application because the officer was not satisfied that the applicant would leave Canada at the end of her authorized stay.

propositions.text: The officer's conclusion was based on two findings.
propositions.quote: The officer based this conclusion on two findings.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the officer refused the application due to doubts about leaving Canada, based on two findings.

propositions.text: Officer found applicant's visit purpose inconsistent with temporary stay due to lack of rationale for leaving stable employment and unclear employment benefit in Ghana.
propositions.quote: First, the officer found that the purpose of the applicant’s visit was not consistent with a temporary stay given the details she had provided in her application. More particularly, the applicant had not established the rationale for leaving her current stable employment as a senior midwife in order to pursue this new credential at high financial cost. As well, the applicant had not established that this credential would provide her with an employment benefit in Ghana.

paragraphs.summary: The officer found the applicant's purpose inconsistent with a temporary stay due to lack of rationale and unclear employment benefit in Ghana.

propositions.text: Officer found applicant had not established sufficient assets and financial situation to support studies in Canada.
propositions.quote: Second, the officer found that applicant had not established that her assets and financial situation were sufficient to support her proposed studies in Canada.

propositions.text: Applicant's husband undertook to cover study costs; applicant provided joint bank statement, Eurobond holdings, and Treasury Bill investments as financial evidence.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s husband had undertaken to cover the costs of the applicant’s studies. To demonstrate that they had the means to fund her studies in Canada, the applicant provided financial information that included the following: (1) a statement for a joint bank account with Ecobank from December 2024 to March 2025 showing transactions over that period and a final balance of $34,185.12 (USD); (2) Eurobond holdings in the amount of $57,981 (USD); and (3) Treasury Bill investments equivalent to $102,769 (CAD).

propositions.text: Applicant prepaid $5,635 towards $9,500 program fee.
propositions.quote: The applicant also provided proof that she had pre-paid $5,635 towards the $9,500 total program fee.

propositions.text: Officer found no evidence on source of husband's Eurobond and Treasury Bill funds, leading to dissatisfaction with sufficiency of funds.
propositions.quote: The officer found, however, that there was no evidence of how the applicant’s husband came to accumulate either the Eurobond holdings or the Treasury Bill savings. The officer wrote: “In the absence of satisfactory documentation showing the source of these funds, I am not satisfied that the applicant will have sufficient funds for the intended international study.”

paragraphs.summary: The officer found insufficient evidence of financial means, especially regarding husband's Eurobond and Treasury Bill funds, to support studies.

propositions.text: Applicant submits the officer's findings are unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The applicant submits that these findings are unreasonable

propositions.text: Court disagrees with applicant's submission that findings are unreasonable.
propositions.quote: but I do not agree.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the findings are unreasonable; the court disagrees.

propositions.text: The program is designed to train internationally educated midwives for practice in Canada and is non-credit with no academic transcripts.
propositions.quote: it should be noted that, as the letter of acceptance submitted by the applicant made clear, the program is designed to train internationally educated midwives for practice in Canada. Significantly, the IEMBP is a non-credit program and it does not issue academic transcripts or attendance records.

propositions.text: Upon completion, a form is sent to BC College of Midwives confirming eligibility to register.
propositions.quote: Instead, upon successful completion, a completion form is sent to the British Columbia College of Midwives confirming that the student has met all the requirements to be eligible to register with the college.

propositions.text: Applicant did not address that the program is meant for midwives wanting to practice in Canada.
propositions.quote: While the applicant said in her study plan that the program would benefit her practice as a midwife in Ghana, she did not directly address the fact that it is meant for midwives who want to practice in Canada.

propositions.text: Little evidence showed the program taught many skills applicant hoped to learn or added meaningfully to her prior training and experience.
propositions.quote: As well, there was little evidence that the program actually taught many of the subjects and skills the applicant said she hoped to learn through the program or how the program would meaningfully add to what the applicant had already learned through her training and work experience in Ghana.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the program is for midwives practicing in Canada; applicant did not address this or show how it added to her skills.

propositions.text: Officer could have explained more about dissatisfaction with applicant's reasons but given information, reasons are sufficient, transparent, intelligible, and justified.
propositions.quote: The officer could certainly have said more about why they were not satisfied with the applicant’s reasons for wanting to pursue this particular program but, given the information the applicant had presented in her study permit application, the reasons that were given are sufficient to explain the officer’s finding in a way that is transparent, intelligible and justified.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer's reasons, though brief, sufficiently explain the dissatisfaction with applicant's reasons.

propositions.text: Officer's concern about sufficiency of funds was not unreasonable given lack of evidence on source of significant funds.
propositions.quote: Second, it was not unreasonable for the officer to be concerned about the sufficiency of the funds that would be available to support the applicant’s studies in Canada given the complete absence of evidence as to the provenance of a significant portion of the funds the applicant relied on in her application.

propositions.text: Applicant's husband stated he was financially sound but no evidence of employment or income was provided.
propositions.quote: While the applicant’s husband stated in his affidavit that he was “financially sound to bear my wife’s entire financial expenses during her stay in Canada,” there was no evidence as to how this was the case – not even whether he was employed.

propositions.text: Applicant had been employed since 2019 but no evidence of income was provided.
propositions.quote: Moreover, while the applicant herself had been employed as a midwife since July 2019, there was no evidence of the income she earned in that position.

propositions.text: Officer's reasons, though could be more detailed, sufficiently explain the finding given the information before the officer.
propositions.quote: Again, while the officer could have said more about this, I am satisfied that what the officer did say, when read in light of the information before the officer, was sufficient to explain their finding.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer's concern about funds reasonable given lack of evidence on source and income, and reasons sufficient.

propositions.text: Applicant argues officer's concern about provenance of funds was unreasonable because joint bank account funds alone suffice.
propositions.quote: The applicant also submits that it was unreasonable for the officer to be concerned about the provenance of the Eurobond holdings and Treasury Bill investments because the funds in the joint bank account alone would be sufficient to cover the costs of her studies in Canada.

propositions.text: Court disagrees; application relied on multiple sources so officer reasonably scrutinized all funds.
propositions.quote: I do not agree. Even if it were true that the joint bank account funds were sufficient (something that is far from obvious given the absence of any evidence of the family’s regular expenses), that is not how the study permit application was presented to the officer. With the applicant herself having seen fit to rely on the additional sources of funds, it was not unreasonable for the officer to scrutinize those funds.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably found evidence of availability of additional funds insufficient.
propositions.quote: Nor was it unreasonable for the officer to find that the evidence that those funds would be available to the applicant was insufficient.

propositions.text: Officer did not comment on sufficiency of joint account funds alone but was not asked to do so; this does not undermine reasonableness.
propositions.quote: While the officer did not comment directly on the sufficiency of the funds in the joint bank account alone, they were never asked to do so. The failure to address the sufficiency of those funds on their own does not undermine the reasonableness of the decision given the financial picture presented by the applicant in support of the study permit application.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues joint account funds suffice; court disagrees and finds officer reasonably scrutinized all funds and decision remains reasonable.

propositions.text: Applicant may reapply with evidence addressing officer's concerns but has not established basis to interfere with decision.
propositions.quote: The applicant was no doubt disappointed with the officer’s decision but she can always apply again for a study permit. If she does, and if she is able to provide evidence that addresses the concerns raised by this officer, she may well be able to satisfy another officer that a study permit should be issued. The applicant has not, however, established any basis on which to interfere with the decision under review.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review must, therefore, be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review but notes applicant may reapply with better evidence.

propositions.text: No serious questions of general importance arise for certification under IRPA paragraph 74(d).
propositions.quote: The parties did not propose any serious questions of general importance for certification under paragraph 74(d) of the IRPA. I agree that no question arises.

propositions.text: Judgment: judicial review dismissed; no question of general importance stated.
propositions.quote: JUDGMENT IN IMM-12386-25 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that The application for judicial review is dismissed. No question of general importance is stated.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no serious question of general importance and dismisses the judicial review application.
